content: Hey, I've got some spare time before going into the second year of my maths degree and I want to contribute to mathlib. Do I have the knowledge yet to actually make a PR? Ive worked through a decent chunk of the natural number game and Ive done some easy proofs on my own PC. If I am ready to start contributing, however small that looks like, how do I get started and where do I find what to work on?

This is not really the right question. This is like saying "I've just learnt python and now I would like to contribute to the python core library". What you mean, I think, is "I have some time to do Lean and I want to make a library which depends on mathlib". Essentially all undergraduate and a lot of graduate level mathematics is already in mathlib, and what is left is missing because it is difficult to do for technical reasons known to the experts.

Kevin, you wrote "Essentially all undergraduate ... mathematics is already in mathlib". However the page Missing undergraduate mathematics in mathlib lists a large number of topics. To be clear, is that page woefully out of date?

I suspect that the reason that page has a lot on it is that it's full of material which we either (a) don't want or (b) want but in a more complex form and is thus a task suitable for an expert.

It would not surprise me if this page had been in this state for years now. The point of my previous message is that all the easy stuff went years ago. Some people have disagreed with this claim in the past and perhaps they'll do so again and point to something which is currently accessible, but basically my view is that the time where an untrained but interested undergrad working alone can helpfully contribute to mathlib is long gone. This does not mean that they cannot contribute to the ecosystem! I am constantly working with undergraduates on projects -- a few weeks ago I had a team of undergraduates classify all groups of order less than 32, and currently I have one putting a Riemannian structure on the sphere. I am specifically talking about contributing to mathlib.
The bottleneck with mathlib is not finding new contributors; this is why we have over 3000 open PRs. The problem with mathlib is that we have too few reviewers.
Is there a way to spread the words "we need more people reviewing PRs"? It seems not obvious for new comers

I think there's lots of undergrad-level stuff to do, but what are your interests?
(although I agree with most of the above)

Even for first year, e.g. #42236 just recently added row echelon form, and of course tons of graph theory is missing.
Also I think we still don't have (A + B).rank ≤ A.rank + B.rank for matrices (just for linear maps in vector spaces), or anything about the det/trace/eigenvalues of the exp of a matrix.

Kevin Buzzard said:

The bottleneck with mathlib is not finding new contributors; this is why we have over 3000 open PRs. The problem with mathlib is that we have too few reviewers.

Reviewing requires some contribution experience in practice.

I think an undergrad formalizing exercises from their course is very likely to find small lemmas missing from mathlib that are useful in practice for applying the material in mathlib to more concrete examples. (Though quite often the review of a PR of such a lemma would point out that actually it's not missing, the mathlib version is just something much more general that a beginner didn't think to look for - so helping them learn mathlib conventions even if it doesn't result in anything getting added to mathlib.)

Joseph Myers said:

I think an undergrad formalizing exercises from their course is very likely to find small lemmas missing from mathlib that are useful in practice for applying the material in mathlib to more concrete examples. (Though quite often the review of a PR of such a lemma would point out that actually it's not missing, the mathlib version is just something much more general that a beginner didn't think to look for - so helping them learn mathlib conventions even if it doesn't result in anything getting added to mathlib.)

As someone who's been formalizing exercises from an undergraduate course for months now, this is definitely the case. You'll find lemmas that you wish were present, but aren't.

As to the second remark, often a very general version of a theorem exists alongside a version that is more specific and more useful. This causes me to be annoyed when I search for the specific version, get the general version, and learn about the specific one later.

Many mathlib lemmas are there for convenience, so I'm not sure why "you can do the same thing in a dozen lines by starting at a much higher level of generality and then carefully beating the perfect abstract sphere into the shape of your problem" would be an obstacle to an additional convenience lemma?

Thanks everyone, these responses are really insightful. I still want to try contributing even if its small, since I think that the process itself will teach me a lot, and as Shreyas pointed out, contribution experience is probably the path toward eventually being able to help with the review bottleneck too. I've been looking through issue #7987 and found some TODOs in the Kleene algebra files, where the mathematical content looks familiar, so I think I'll start there. And then I might also take the suggestion of trying to formalize some exercises from my course and just seeing what is missing that way. Also to Snir's point, linear algebra is a module I found particularly interesting, so I appreciate that suggestion and I will definitely look in that direction.
